faqs.a: Use the Compress button again after changing quality. There is no extra penalty: each run re-encodes from your original file, not from the last compressed copy.
faqs.q: Can I compress the same image twice?

faqs.a: Yes. Pick a smaller max width (for example 1600 pixels) and a quality around 70 to 80. The tool resizes first, then compresses, so you get a small file that still looks good on screens.
faqs.q: How do I make the file really tiny?

faqs.a: The quality slider is ignored for PNG because PNG compression is lossless - it only applies to JPEG and WebP. PNGs shrink mostly by resizing to smaller dimensions.
faqs.q: Why does quality not change my PNG?

faqs.a: For photos: JPEG at 75 to 85 percent quality is the sweet spot. WebP gives about 25 to 30 percent smaller files than JPEG at the same look - use it when the destination supports it.
faqs.q: JPEG or WebP - which should I choose?

faqs.a: Lossy compression throws away fine detail permanently, so text-heavy screenshots can blur below quality 60. Keep the original and stay above 70 for anything you need to read.

image-compressor.formula:
savings % = (original bytes - compressed bytes) / original bytes x 100
resize: new height = original height x (max width / original width)
Example: a 4000 x 3000 photo limited to 1600 wide:
scale = 1600 / 4000 = 0.4 -> 1600 x 1200 pixels.
howTo: Choose an image file up to 50 MB - JPG, PNG, WebP, GIF, BMP or SVG.
Pick an output format: JPEG (photos), WebP (smallest) or PNG (lossless).
Drag the quality slider. Around 80 percent looks identical for most photos.
Set a max width if you also want to shrink the dimensions.
Press Compress, check the before and after sizes, then download.
keyFacts: JPEG and WebP use lossy compression: lower quality means a smaller file with more artefacts.
PNG uses lossless compression: the quality slider has no effect on PNG output.
Resizing dimensions shrinks files far more than lowering quality - a 4000-pixel photo halved in width has a quarter of the pixels.
JPEG cannot store transparency: transparent areas become white.
WebP is about 25 to 30 percent smaller than JPEG at equal visual quality.
This tool re-encodes from your original file every time, so repeated tries never degrade quality.

image-compressor.quickAnswer: Upload a photo, set a quality (around 80 percent is the sweet spot), pick JPEG or WebP output and optionally shrink the width. A typical 2.4 MB phone photo at 1600 pixels wide and 80 percent JPEG quality becomes roughly 480 KB - about 80 percent smaller with no visible difference. Everything happens in your browser, so the photo is never uploaded.
image-compressor.tagline: Shrink JPG, PNG and WebP photos in seconds - with quality and size control.
image-compressor.workedExample:
Take a 4000 x 3000 phone photo, 2.4 MB, and compress it to JPEG at 80 percent quality with a max width of 1600.
1. Resize: scale = 1600 / 4000 = 0.4. New size = 1600 x 1200 pixels.
2. Pixels drop from 12 million to 1.92 million - six times fewer.
3. JPEG re-encodes at quality 80, typically around 480 KB for this kind of photo.
4. Savings = (2.4 - 0.48) / 2.4 x 100 = 80%.
Exact results vary by photo detail, but 70 to 85 percent savings are normal at these settings.
